label: lem:alternatedefinition
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Fixing any orientation of $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$, the number of sheets meeting along a singular arc $K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ of an oriented folded surface $X$ is $\sum_{B \in \pi_0(q^{-1}(K))} |\deg(q_B)|$ (equal to the number of sheets of the $S^1$ covering $q^{-1}[K]\xrightarrow{q} K$). Let $[B]\in H_1(\partial{X_{cut}})$ be the fundamental class of the boundary component $B$ (with induced orientation) and $[K]$ be the fundamental class of the component $K$ in $H_1(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X);\mathbb{Z})$. The induced homomorphism $H_1(\partial{X_{cut}};\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_1(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X);\mathbb{Z})$ sends $[B] \mapsto \deg(q_B)[K]$. Note that clearly $[\partial{X_{cut}}] = \sum_{B \in \pi_0(\partial{X_{cut}})}[B]$ and $[\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)] = \sum_{K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))} [K]$. Also, $\partial{X_{cut}}$ is a disjoint union of the sets $q^{-1}(K)$ for all $K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$. Together this implies that the induced homomorphism sends $[\partial{X_{cut}}] \mapsto \sum_{K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))}\left[\sum_{B\in \pi_0(q^{-1}(K))} \deg(q_B)\right][K]$. It is now easy to verify from these facts that conditions~\eqref{altdef:degpositive} and~\eqref{altdef:sumdegp} of Lemma~\ref{lem:alternatedefinition} are equivalent to the two properties in Definition~\ref{dfn:pfoldedsurface}.

label: lem:regularneighbourhoods
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:regularneighbourhoods}
    If $X$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface then for all $K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ a regular neighbourhood of $K$ in $X$ is homeomorphic to $[0,1]\times K_{p,1} / \sim$ where $(1,x) \sim (0,f(x))$ where $f\in \text{Aut}(K_{p,1})= \text{Sym}(p)$. The homeomorphism type is classified by the cycle type of $f$ and equivalently the multiset $\{\deg(q_B)\}_{B\in \pi_0(q^{-1}(K))}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: A regular neighbourhood $N(K)$ of $K\in \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ must be homeomorphic to a PL fibre bundle of the graph $K_{p,1}$ over $S^1$. Such a fibre bundle can be assembled using the fact that each boundary component $B$ of $X_{cut}$ collars in $X_{cut}$ and that if $q_{X}(B) = K$ then the restriction of $q_{X}$ to $B$ is a covering map of the circle. Thus, there exists a homeomorphism $f\in \text{Homeo}(K_{p,1})$ with isotopy class $[f] \in \text{Aut}(K_{p,1}) = \pi_0(\text{Homeo}(K_{p,1}))= \text{Sym}(p)$ such that $N(K) \simeq [0,1]\times K_{p,1} / \sim$ where $(1,x) \sim (0,f(x))$. The isomorphism class of this fibre bundle over $S^1$ is determined by the conjugacy class of $[f]\in \pi_0(\text{Homeo}(K_{p,1}))$ which is equivalent to its cycle type as an element of $\text{Sym}(p)$. The identification with the symmetric group is given by labelling the $p$ valence $1$ vertices $\{v_1,\ldots v_p\}$ which are permuted by the graph isomorphism by $v_i\mapsto v_{f(i)}$. We define the cycle type to be the partition of $p$ given by writing an element of $\text{Sym}(p)$ as a product of cycles featuring each of $\{1,\ldots, p\}$ exactly once and taking the multiset of cycle lengths. We will now show that this multiset is independent of the choice of fibre bundle and so determines the homeomorphism type. Let $N_{cut}(K)$ be the disjoint union of annuli given by cutting $N(K)$ along $K$. For each $A \in \pi_0(N_{cut}(K))$ the map $A \rightarrow N(K)$ induces the homomorphism $H_1(A;\mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_1(N(K);\mathbb{Z})$ given by $a\mapsto k_A[K]$ for some choice of generating class $\langle a \rangle = H_1(A;\mathbb{Z})$ and a positive integer $k_A$. The multiset $\{k_A\}_{A\in \pi_0(N\setminus K)}$ is equivalent to the cycle type of $f$ since $k_A$ is determined by the size of $\{v_1,\ldots v_p\} \cap \text{im}(A)$. $N_{cut}(K)$ is homeomorphic to a collar neighbourhood of $q^{-1}(K) \subset \partial{X_{cut}}$ and the multiset $\{k_A\}_{A\in \pi_0(N\setminus K)}$ can also be computed from the degrees of the maps $B \xrightarrow{q} q(B)$ for each $B$ in the preimage of $K$. This gives the desired classification of the homeomorphism type of $N(K)$ by the multiset $\{\deg(q_B)\}_{B\in \pi_0(q^{-1}(K))}$.

label: dfn:pfoldgraph
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{dfn:pfoldgraph}
    A \textit{$p$-fold graph} $G$ is a finite bipartite multi-graph 
    \[ G = (I,S,E,\phi,\psi,d,g)\]
    with vertex sets $I,S$, edges $E$ and edge endpoints given by the functions $\phi:E\rightarrow I$ and $\psi:E\rightarrow S$ together with edge labels $d:E\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{>0}$ and vertex labels $g:I\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}$ such that $\sum_{e\in \psi^{-1}(s)} d(e) =p$. An isomorphism of $p$-fold graphs is an isomorphism of bipartite multi-graphs that preserves labels and partitions.

label: def:assocgraph
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $p>0$. The homeomorphism class of any $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $(X,\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ is determined by the isomorphism class of $G(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The associated graph described in Definition~\ref{def:assocgraph} depends only on the topology of a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface and is independent of the choice of orientation. Hence homeomorphic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surfaces have isomorphic $p$-fold graphs.

    To prove the converse, suppose that we have two $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surfaces $X, \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ and $Y,\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y)$ and an isomorphism $f:G(X) \rightarrow G(Y)$. Let $G(X) := (I,S,E,\phi,\psi,d,g)$ and $G(Y) := (I',S',E',\phi',\psi',d',g')$. Fix an orientation preserving homeomorphism $h:\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)\rightarrow \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y)$ such that for all $K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ we have $f(K) = \text{im}(h|_K)$. Now let $q_X:X_{cut}\rightarrow X$ and $q_Y:Y_{cut}\rightarrow Y$ be the two projection maps described in Section~\ref{sec:regnbhds}. Since $h$ is orientation preserving and $f$ is a $p$-fold graph isomorphism we have that $\deg(q_X|_{B}) = \deg(q_Y|_{f(B)})$ and $\text{im}(q_Y|_{f(B)}) = \text{im}(h\circ q_X|_{B})$ so we can use the lifting criterion for each component to construct a homeomorphism $\tilde{h}:\partial X_{cut}\rightarrow \partial{Y_{cut}}$ which commutes with the projection maps for all $B\in \pi_0(\partial{X_{cut}})$:

\begin{center}
    \begin{tikzcd}
        B \ar[r, "\tilde{h}"] \ar[d, "q_{B}"] 
        & 
        f(B) \ar[d, "q_{f(B)}"] 
        \\
        \psi(B) \ar[r, "h"] 
        & 
        \psi'(f(B)) = f(\psi(B))
    \end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

    Note that the definition of a $p$-fold graph isomorphism implies that $\psi'\circ f= f\circ \psi $, $\phi'\circ f  = f\circ \phi$, $g' \circ f = g$ and $d' \circ f = d$. The second fact tells us that if we take $X_i\in \pi_0(X_{cut})$ and $Y_i = f(X_i) \in \pi_0(Y_{cut})$ then $\tilde{h}$ restricts to a homeomorphism $\tilde{h}:\partial{X_i}\rightarrow \partial{Y_i}$ preserving the induced orientation on the boundary. The third fact tells us that the genus of $X_i$ is the same as the genus of $Y_i$. It is well known (for example see Theorem 1 of~\cite{youngs:1948}) that $\tilde{h}$ can be extended to a homeomorphism from $X_i\rightarrow Y_i$ and hence a homeomorphism $\tilde{h}:X_{cut}\rightarrow Y_{cut}$. By construction this descends to a homeomorphism $h:X\rightarrow Y$ which extends the original $h:\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)\rightarrow \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y)$ over the interior.

label: lem:classificationin3mflds
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:classificationin3mflds}
    Let $X$ be a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface such that $p$ is prime and let $G(X) = (I,S,E,\phi,\psi,d,g)$ be its associated graph. $X$ can be embedded in an orientable $3$-manifold if and only if $d(B) \in \{1,p\}\ \forall\ B\in E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, let $X$ be a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface embedded in a $3$-manifold $M$ and let $S$ be any singular arc of $X$. We will prove that for every component $B$ of $q^{-1}(S)$ the degree of $B\rightarrow S$ is $1$ or $p$. 

    Let $N(S)$ be a regular neighbourhood of $S$ in $M$ such that $N(S)\cap X$ is a regular neighbourhood of $S$ in $X$. By gluing together the product structure $(K_{p,1},\mathbb{D}^2)\times \mathbb{R}$ of neighbourhoods of points on $S$ we can assemble a fibre bundle $\mathbb{D}^2 \rightarrow N(S) \rightarrow S^1$ with sub-bundle $K_{p,1}\rightarrow N(S)\cap X \rightarrow S^1$. The restriction of the embedding $N(S)\cap X \rightarrow N(S)$ on fibres is the embedding $K_{p,1}\subset \mathbb{D}^2$ in Figure~\ref{fig:subbundle}.
    
    The embedding $N(S)\cap X \hookrightarrow N(S)$ is therefore homeomorphic to an embedding of mapping tori $K_{p,1}\times[0,1]/\sim \hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2 \times [0,1]/\sim$ where $(1,x) \sim (0,f(x))$ and $f$ is a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{D}^2$ which restricts to a homeomorphism of $K_{p,1}$. The orientability of $M$ forces $f$ to be orientation preserving. The embedding $K_{p,1}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2$ forces $f|_{K_{p,1}}$ to preserve the cyclic order of the vertices of $K_{p,1}\cap \partial{\mathbb{D}^2}$. The graph isomorphism class $[f|_{K_{p,1}}]\in \text{Sym}(p)$ must therefore be a cyclic permutation of order dividing $p$. If $[f|_{K_{p,1}}]=id$ then $\forall B \in \pi_0(q^{-1}(S))$ the map $q_B:B \rightarrow S$ has degree $1$, and we will call $S$ \textit{straight} if this is the case. If $[f|_{K_{p,1}}]\neq id$ then its order is $p$ and so $\pi_0(q^{-1}(S)) = \{B\}$, $q_B:B \rightarrow S$ has degree $p$ and we call $S$ \textit{twisted}.

    Now suppose $X$ is such a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface with the property that $d(e) \in \{1,p\}\ \forall\ e\in E$. Let $S\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ and $N(S)$ be a regular neighbourhood of $S$ in $X$. The fact that $\sum_{e\in \psi^{-1}(S)} d(e) =p$ implies that either $|\psi^{-1}(S)| = p$ and $d(B)= 1\ \forall\ B\in \psi^{-1}(S)$ ($S$ is \textit{straight}) or $\psi^{-1}(S) = \{B\}$ and $d(B)=p$ ($S$ is \textit{twisted}). Consider the embedding $K_{p,1} \simeq \{te^{2i\pi k/p}, k \in \{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}, t \in [0,1]\}$ in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}^2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:regularneighbourhoods} implies that $N(S)$ is homeomorphic to $[0,1]\times K_{p,1}/\sim$ where $(1,x) \sim (0,f(x))$ and $f:K_{p,1}\rightarrow K_{p,1}$ is the restriction of $id\in \text{Aut}(\mathbb{C})$ if $S$ is straight or $z \mapsto ze^{2i\pi/p}$ if $S$ is twisted. In both cases we can use the embedding of $K_{p,1}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2$ to construct an embedding of $N(S)\hookrightarrow T(S)$ where $T(S)$ is the solid torus $[0,1]\times \mathbb{D}^2/\sim$ where $(1,x) \sim (0,f(x))$. Now repeat this for all $S\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$ and let $N(X) := \bigsqcup_{S\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))}N(S)$ and $T(X):= \bigsqcup_{S\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))}T(S)$. Let $\Sigma(X)$ be the compact orientable $2$-manifold which is the closure in $X$ of $X \setminus \bigsqcup_{S\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))} N(S)$. $\partial{\Sigma(X)}$ is a $1$-manifold identified in $X$ with $\partial{N(X)} = \partial{T(X)} \cap N(X)$. Thicken $[-1,1]\times \Sigma(X)$ such that $\Sigma(X) = \{0\} \times \Sigma(X)$. We then extend the homeomorphism identifying $\{0\} \times \partial \Sigma(X)$ with $N(X) \cap \partial T(X)$ to a homeomorphism identifying $[-1,1]\times \partial \Sigma(X)$ with the disjoint union of annuli that form a regular neighbourhood of $N(X) \cap \partial T(X)$ in the disjoint union of tori $\partial T(X)$. The result is an embedding of $X$ in the compact orientable $3$-manifold with boundary $T(X)\sqcup [-1,1]\times \Sigma(X)/\sim$ with image $N(X)\sqcup \Sigma(X)/\sim$, where $\sim$ denotes the identification described above.

label: lem:existence
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $M$ be a compact orientable $3$-manifold. Every homology class $x\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ can be represented by a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface.
    \label{lem:existence}
head: environment
name: Existence

title: Proof
body_md:
The main idea for this proof comes from Lemma 2.1 of~\cite{Turaevfnhom3mfld2007}, which we supplement with a surgery on a regular neighbourhood of $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ required to obtain a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface rather than a general simple folded surface. We also relax part of Turaev's construction by allowing $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ to be any oriented link representing $d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x)$ rather than requiring a knot. This change is not strictly necessary for existence but it allows Lemma~\ref{lem:thurstonnorm} in Section~\ref{sec:zpthurstonnorm} to follow relatively easily. Existence can also be shown constructively using a technique analogous to normal surface theory which we develop in Section~\ref{sec:canonicalpfoldedsurfaces}.
    
    We start by choosing an oriented link $L$ embedded via $l:L\rightarrow M$ such that $i_{(M,L)}([L]) = d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x)$. Note that the coefficient long exact sequence and the long exact sequence of the pair are both natural. For the reader's convenience we assemble the part of the large commutative diagram that they form together which is relevant to the proof in Equation~\eqref{cd:bigcd}.


\begin{equation}\label{cd:bigcd}
    \resizebox{0.88\linewidth}{!}{ 
        $\begin{tikzcd}[
            cramped,
            column sep=small,
            row sep=normal,
            ampersand replacement=\&
        ]
            H_2(L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_2(M;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"j_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"i_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(M;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
            \\
            H_2(L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_2(M;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"j_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(L;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
                \ar[r,"i_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(M;\mathbb{Z})
                \ar[d,"j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"]
            \\
            H_2(L;\mathbb{Z}_p)
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)
                \ar[r,"j_{(M,L)}"]
                \ar[uurrr,
                    rounded corners=4pt,
                    "d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}"{pos=0.75},
                    to path={
                        (\tikztostart.south)
                        -- ++(0,-8mm)
                        -| ([xshift=10mm]\tikztotarget.east)
                        \tikztonodes
                        -- (\tikztotarget.east)
                    }
                ]
            \&
            H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z}_p)
                \ar[r,"d_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(L;\mathbb{Z}_p)
                \ar[r,"i_{(M,L)}"]
            \&
            H_1(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)
        \end{tikzcd}$ 
    }
\end{equation}



    The exactness of the coefficient long exact sequence implies that $0 = i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}\circ d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x) = i_{\mathbb{Z}_p} \circ i_{(M,L)}([L])$.
    The coefficient long exact sequence and the relative homology long exact sequence are natural and so $i_{(M,L)} \circ i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}([L]) = 0$. The exactness of the long exact sequence of the pair implies that there exists a class $x' \in H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z})$ such that $d_{(M,L)}(x') = i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}([L]) = p\cdot [L]$. A dimension argument implies that $H_2(L;\mathbb{Z}_p)=0$ so it follows that $j_{(M,L)}:H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)\rightarrow H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is injective. The naturality of the two sequences implies that $d_{(M,L)}(j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x')) = j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(d_{(M,L)}(x')) = j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}\circ i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}([L]) = 0$ and so there is a unique lift $x'' := j_{(M,L)}^{-1}(j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x')) \in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ of $j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x')$. 
    
    It follows from a chase over the commutative diagram~\eqref{cd:bigcd} or alternatively from the definition of the connecting homomorphism that $d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x'') = d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x) = [L]$. Therefore there must exist some $y\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z})$ such that $x = j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(y) + x''$. Let $x''' := j_{(M,L)}(y) + x' \in H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z})$ such that $j^{-1}_{(M,L)}(j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x''')) = x$. 

    Take an open regular neighbourhood $N$ of $L$. By excision and deformation we can identify $H_2(M,L;\mathbb{Z})= H_2(M,\overline{N};\mathbb{Z}) = H_2(M\setminus N,\partial(N);\mathbb{Z})$. It is well known that every integral 2-homology class of a compact oriented 3-manifold such as $M \setminus N$ is represented by a properly embedded oriented surface. Let $S$ be such a surface where $[S] = x''' \in H_2(M\setminus N(L),\partial(N(L));\mathbb{Z})$. Consider the maps on homology induced by the embedding $f:(M\setminus N,\partial(N)) \hookrightarrow (M,\overline{N})$ and the naturality of the long exact sequence of relative homology.

    \begin{center}
        \begin{tikzcd}
        H_2(M\setminus N,\partial(N);\mathbb{Z}) \ar[r,"d"] \ar[d,"f_*"] 
        & H_1(\partial(N);\mathbb{Z}) \ar[d,"f_*"] 
        \\
        H_2(M,\overline{N};\mathbb{Z}) \ar[r,"d"]
        & H_1(\overline{N};\mathbb{Z})
        \end{tikzcd}
    \end{center}

    $\partial(N)$ is a disjoint union of tori and we can choose generators $\lambda_k$ and $\mu_k$ represented by simple closed curves on $\partial(N_k)$ for each component $N_k$ of $N$. Let $L_k$ be the component of $L$ that is a core circle of $N_k$. Let $\mu_k, \lambda_k$ be generators of $H_1(\partial(N_k);\mathbb{Z})$ such that $\mu_k$ generates $\ker(f_*)\cap H_1(\partial(N_k);\mathbb{Z})$ and $f_*(\lambda_k) = [L_k]$. The above commutative square can be used to show that $\partial(S)\cap \partial(N_k)$ is a union of oriented simple closed curves with homology class $p_k\lambda_k + q_k\mu_k \in H_1(\partial(N_k);\mathbb{Z})$. Null-homologous curves on the torus bound a disk and so can be eliminated by pasting a disk parallel to $\partial N_k$. After all null-homologous curves are removed $\partial(S)\cap \partial(N_k)$ is a disjoint union of simple closed curves of equal slope, a consequence of the fact that the intersection form is trivial on primitive non-trivial $s_1,s_2 \in H_1(\mathbb{T}^2;\mathbb{Z})$ classes only if $s_1 = \pm s_2$. If the curves are not oriented consistently then there must exist an annulus embedded in $\partial(N_k)$ cobounding two curves of opposite orientation. We can again perform a local surgery to $S$ by gluing an annulus with the required orientation in the interior of $M\setminus N$ parallel to the annulus in the boundary to remove these two components of $\partial(S)$ without changing the homology class represented by $S$. Once these surgeries are complete it follows that $\partial S \cap \partial N_k$ is a $(p_k,q_k)$-torus link where every component represents the same homology class. This torus link is unique up to an isotopy of $\partial N_k$ which the PL isotopy extension theorem allows us to extend to an isotopy of $N_k$. We can therefore obtain a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X$ by setting $X\cap M\setminus N := S$ and $X\cap N_k \subset N_k$ to be a PL-approximation of the embedding where $N_k = \mathbb{C} \times [0,1]/\sim$ where $(z,0)\sim (z,1)$ and $X\cap N_k = \bigcup_{j=0}^{p} \{x e^{(j+q_{k}t)/2ip_{k}\pi}\ |\ x \in \mathbb{R}, t\in [0,1]\}/\sim$. This model neighbourhood of a singular arc is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:modelsingularnbhd}. 

    $x'''$ is the image of the fundamental class of $(X_{cut},\partial X_{cut})$ in $(M,\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X))$. By definition the fundamental class of $X$ is the unique lift of $j_{(M,L)}^{-1}(j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}([X_{cut}]))$. It follows that the image of this fundamental class in $M$ is $j_{(M,L)}^{-1}(j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x''')) = x$ completing the proof.

label: lem:nonorientable
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nonorientable}
    Definition~\ref{dfn:z2thurstonnorm} and Definition~\ref{dfn:zpthurstonnorm} are equivalent when $p=2$ and $M$ is a closed $3$-manifold.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will use $||\cdot||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}$ to refer to the function in Definition~\ref{dfn:z2thurstonnorm} and $||\cdot||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}'$ to refer to the function in Definition~\ref{dfn:zpthurstonnorm}
    
    Suppose $\Sigma$ is an unoriented surface realising $x$ such that 
    \[||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2} = \sum_{\Sigma_0\in \pi_0(\Sigma)} \max(0, -\chi(\Sigma_0)).\] 
    First we choose a system of disjoint closed curves suggestively named $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$, embedded in $\Sigma$ such that $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ is an orientable $2$-manifold with the same number of connected components as $\Sigma$. This can be achieved by the following induction. We start with $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma) = \emptyset$. At each step if $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ is non-orientable, it is possible to find a simple closed curve $C$ whose neighbourhood in $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ is a Mobius band. Being the core circle of a Mobius band, $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma) \setminus C$ must have the same number of components as $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$. Hence we add $C$ to $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ and repeat. Since $2 |\pi_0(\Sigma)| - |\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)|$ gives an upper bound on $\chi(\Sigma)$ it follows that this induction must terminate with $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ having the desired properties. Now choose some arbitrary orientation of $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ and view it as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface. The components of $\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma)$ respectively have the same Euler characteristic as the components of $\Sigma$ that contain them. Hence the following is true:
    
    \[||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2} = \sum_{\Sigma_0\in \pi_0(\Sigma)} \max(0, -\chi(\Sigma_0)) = \sum_{\Sigma_0' \in \pi_0(\Sigma \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\Sigma))} \max(0 , -\chi(\Sigma_0')) \geq ||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}'.\]

    Since the class $[\Sigma] \in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_2)$ does not depend on whether $\Sigma$ is viewed as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface or an unoriented surface it follows that $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2} \geq ||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}'$. 
    
    For the other inequality, let $X$ be a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface embedded in a closed orientable 3-manifold such that $\chi_-(X) = ||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}$. If any component $S \in \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ has a neighbourhood in $X$ homeomorphic to an annulus and bounds a disk, then we can reverse the orientation of the disk and remove $S$ from $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ to obtain a new $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface $X'$ such that $[X'] = [X]$ and $\chi_-(X') \leq \chi_-(X)$. Reassigning $X := X'$ and repeating this procedure we may assume that $X$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface in which the closure of any disk component of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^2$ and we still have $\chi_-(X) = ||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}$. The only other components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$ with positive Euler characteristic are $2$-spheres. We can view $X$ as an unoriented surface simply by forgetting about $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$. Let $X_0$ be a connected component of the unoriented surface $X$. It follows that:

    \[\max(0,-\chi(X_0)) = \sum_{X_0' \in \pi_0(X_0 \setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X_0))} \max(0,-\chi(X_0')).\]

    Globally, this implies the other inequality $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2} \leq ||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_2}'$, completing the proof.

body_md:
\label{dfn:weightedfolded}
    A \textit{weighted oriented folded surface} $X$ is an oriented folded surface $\underline{X}$ together with a positive integer $w_I$ associated to each component $I$ of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X})$. If $X$ is embedded in an orientable $3$-manifold then there exists a related unweighted oriented folded surface $X^u \subset M$ which can be constructed by the following procedure for each $I\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X}))$. Since both $M$ and $I$ are oriented, the 1-dimensional normal bundle of $I$ in $M$ is trivial. This means that $I$ can be pushed in a normal direction, fixing the complement of $I$ in $X$, to obtain $w_I$ parallel copies with the same singular boundary $\partial(I)$. These are completely disjoint if $\partial(I) = \emptyset$. For each $I\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X}))$ replace $I$ with these parallel copies to obtain $X^u$. If $X^u$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface for some choice of orientation of $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X^u) = \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X})$ then we say that $X$ is a \textit{weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface}. To avoid confusion we will write $\underline{X}$ when we are referring to the oriented folded surface obtained from $X$ by forgetting the weights. This is not to be confused with the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X^u$ in general but note that $\underline{X} = X^u$ in the special case when every weight is equal to $1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof adapted from \cite[Lemma IV.3.4]{Turaev2002torsions}, which is the analogue of Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} for \textit{weighted surfaces}. Let $X$ be a weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface. Let $N$ be a component of the complement of $\underline{X}$ in $M$. If $M \setminus \underline{X}$ is not connected, then $\partial(\overline{N}) \neq \emptyset$. Let $\alpha_+$ (resp. $\alpha_-$) be the subset of $\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X}))$ given by the components on the boundary of $\overline{N}$ such that their orientation in $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X})$ is the same as (resp. opposite to) the orientation of $\partial(\overline{N})$ induced by the orientation of $M$.  Now if $\alpha_{-} = \emptyset$ or $\sum_{I\in \alpha_{+}} \chi_-(I) \geq \sum_{J\in \alpha_{-} } \chi_-(J)$ then decrease each $w_{I\in \alpha_+}$ and increase each $w_{J\in \alpha_{-}}$ by $\text{min}\{w_I |I\in \alpha_+\}$. Otherwise, in the case where $\alpha_- \neq \emptyset$ and $\sum_{I\in \alpha_{+}} \chi_-(I) < \sum_{J\in \alpha_{-} } \chi_-(J)$, then increase each $w_{I\in \alpha_+}$ and decrease each $w_{J\in \alpha_-}$ by $\text{min}\{w_J |J\in \alpha_-\}$. Remove any components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X})$ whose weights become $0$ from $\underline{X}$ and denote the resulting weighted oriented folded surface $Y$. The embedding of $(\underline{Y},\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{Y}))$ in $M$ factors through the embedding of $(\underline{X},\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X}))$ in $M$. We can therefore abuse notation to denote by $[X],[Y]$ the fundamental classes of $X$ and $Y$ in $H_2(\underline{X};\mathbb{Z}_p)$. It follows from the construction of $Y$ that $m_*([X] - [Y]) \in H_2(\underline{X},\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X});\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is an integer multiple of $\sum_{I\in \alpha_+}[I] - \sum_{J\in \alpha_-}[J]$ and hence $[X] - [Y]$ is an integer multiple of $[\partial \overline{N}]$, $H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ class of the $2$-cycle boundary of $N$. It follows from definition~\ref{dfn:realisation} that $X$ and $Y$ represent equivalent classes in $H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ since $[\partial \overline{N}]$ is annihilated by the map induced by $X\hookrightarrow M$.
    
    To see that $Y$ is a weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface and that $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X) = \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y)$ simply note that all the components of $Y^u$ still induce consistent orientations on the singular locus and that the long exact sequence of the pair $(\underline{X},\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X}))$ implies that $\sum_{I\in \alpha_{+}}[\partial(I)] = \sum_{J\in \alpha_{-} }[\partial(J)]  \in H_1(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X}))$ and so there is no change in the total number of sheets of $Y^u$ identified along each singular arc. The method by which weights are changed implies that $\chi_-(Y^u)\leq \chi_-(X^u)$. It also follows from the construction that $M\setminus \underline{Y}$ has strictly fewer components than $M\setminus \underline{X}$.
    
    Iterating this process we eventually obtain a weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ such that $M\setminus \underline{Y}$ is connected, satisfying the required properties. 

    The proof is completed by noting that for any $x\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ and $\underline{X}$ a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface that is optimal in the sense that $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p} = \chi_-(\underline{X})$ we can assign weights $w_I = 1$ for all $I \in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X}))$ to obtain a weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X$ such that $X^u = \underline{X}$ and hence $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p} = \chi_-(X^u)$. By following the above induction the resulting weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ must also have the property that $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p} = \chi_-(Y^u)$ (this follows from the definition of $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$) and the additional property that $M\setminus \underline{Y}$ is connected.

title: Proof
body_md:
The implication $\text{\ref{enum:nonseparating}} \Leftrightarrow \text{\ref{enum:Zinjective}}$ can be derived from the long exact sequence of the pair $(M,Y)$ as follows.

    The number of components of $M\setminus Y$ is equal to the rank of $H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$ by taking each component to be a free generator. $H_3(Y;\mathbb{Z})=0$ by a dimension argument and so $j_{(M,Y)}:H_3(M;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$ is injective and so $\ker(H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})) = H_3(M;\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. $H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion free so we can deduce that the kernel of $H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})$ is generated by a primitive element of $H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$. It follows from the first isomorphism theorem that $\operatorname{Im}(H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z}))$ is a free abelian group of rank one less than the rank of $H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$. It follows immediately that $\ker(H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z})) = 0$ if and only if $M\setminus Y$ has a single connected component.

    We can now prove the implication $\text{\ref{enum:Zinjective}} \Leftrightarrow \text{\ref{enum:Zkinjective}}$ by demonstrating both contrapositives.

    Suppose $\ker(H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}))$ is non-trivial, then the above arguments imply that it contains a primitive element $x\in H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})$. This primitive element cannot be in the image of $i_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$ which consists only of non-primitive elements in the subgroup $p \cdot H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})$. Hence $j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x)\neq 0$. But since 
    \[0 = j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}\circ i_{(M,Y)}(x) =  i_{(M,Y)}\circ j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x)\] 
    it follows that 
    \[j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x) \in \ker(H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z}_p)\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)).\] 

    Now suppose that $x$ is a non-trivial element of $\ker(H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z}_p)\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p))$. Lift $x$ to $x'\in H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ such that $d_{(M,Y)}(x') = x$. It follows from excising an open neighbourhood $N(Y)$ of $Y$ that $H_2(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$ is isomorphic to $H_2(M\setminus N(Y),\partial N(Y);\mathbb{Z})$. By Poincar\'e-Lefschetz duality 
    \[H_2(M\setminus N(Y),\partial N(Y);\mathbb{Z}) \simeq H^1(M\setminus N(Y);\mathbb{Z}).\] 
    The universal coefficient theorem implies that 
    \[H^1(M\setminus N(Y);\mathbb{Z}) \simeq \text{Hom}(H_1(M\setminus N(Y);\mathbb{Z}), \mathbb{Z})\] 
    which must be torsion free. We therefore deduce that $H_2(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion free. 
    
    Hence $d_{\mathbb{Z}_p}:H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z}_p) \rightarrow H_2(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$ annihilates all of $H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z}_p)$. It follows that $j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}:H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is a surjection and so $x' = j_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(x'')$ for some $x'' \in H_3(M,Y;\mathbb{Z})$. Since $x = d_{(M,Y)} \circ j_{\mathbb{Z}_p} (x'') =  j_{\mathbb{Z}_p} \circ d_{(M,Y)} (x'')$ it follows that $d_{(M,Y)} (x'') \neq 0$. The exactness of the sequence of the pair $(M,Y)$ implies that $d_{(M,Y)} (x'') \in \ker(H_2(Y;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}))$. This completes the proof.

label: lem:weightp/2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weightp/2}
    If $X$ is a weighted non-separating $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface and $C\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X}))$ is a component with weight $w_C>p/2$ then $C$ is removable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $C$ be any non-compact component of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X})$ such that $w_C>p/2$. Let $C_{cut}$ be the component of $\underline{X}_{cut}$ that is the closure of $q_{\underline{X}}^{-1}(C)$. For any $K\in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X}))$ let $B(C,K)$ be the set of boundary components of $C_{cut}$ mapped to $K$ by $q_{\underline{X}}$. The construction of $X^u$ induces homeomorphisms from $C$ to its $w_C$ parallel copies $C^i$ which extend uniquely to homeomorphisms of $C_{cut}\rightarrow C^i_{cut}$. This allows us to describe disjoint sets $B^u\subset \pi_0(\partial{X^u_{cut}})$ of the $w_C$ boundary components identified with $B \in B(C,K)$ by these homeomorphisms. The construction also implies that $q_{X^u}(\mathcal{B}) = q_{\underline{X}}(B) = K$ and that $\deg(\mathcal{B}\xrightarrow{q_{X^u}} K) = \deg(B\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}}K)$ for all $\mathcal{B}\in B^u$. Summing the degrees of the corresponding maps to $K$, Lemma~\ref{lem:alternatedefinition} implies that $p = \sum_{\mathcal{B} \in \pi_0(q_{X^u}^{-1}(K))} \deg(\mathcal{B}\xrightarrow{q_{X^u}}K) \geq \sum_{\mathcal{B}\in B^u}\sum_{B\in B(C,K)}\deg(B\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} K) = \sum_{B\in B(C,K)}\deg(B\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} K)\cdot w_C$. If $w_C>p/2$ then this inequality implies that $\deg(B\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} K) = 1$ and $|B(C,K)| = 1$ for all $K\in \pi_0(q_{\underline{X}}(\partial C_{cut}))$. This shows that each boundary component of $C_{cut}$ is mapped homeomorphically onto a distinct component of $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X})$ and so $\partial{C_{cut}}\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(\underline{X})$ is an embedding. It is already known that $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{C}_{cut})\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} C \subset \operatorname{\text{Int}}(\underline{X})$ is a homeomorphism. Together this implies that $C_{cut}\xrightarrow{q_{\underline{X}}} \underline{X}$ is an embedding, proving the claim.

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof is similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:noremovabledisks}, but we need to be a bit more careful with orientation in the construction and the $\chi_-$ of $X$ and $Y$. It will be sufficient to find a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y'$ such that $[X] = [Y']$, $\chi_-(Y') \leq \chi_-(X^u)$ and $|\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y'))| = |\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X^u))|- |\pi_0(\partial{C})|$ since we can use Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} to collapse $Y'$ onto a non-separating weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ such that $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y) = \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y')$ and $\chi_-(Y^u)\leq \chi_-(Y')$. Additionally, if $w_C = p$ the proof is trivial by simply deleting $\overline{C}$ from the components of $X$ to obtain $Y$ so we assume that $p/2<w_C<p$ in the following.
    
    Let $\{C_i\}_{i=1}^{w_C}$ be the components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X^u)$ parallel to $C$ as per the construction of $X^u$ from $\underline{X}$. Remove the components $\{C_i\}_{i=p-w_C+1}^{w_C}$ and reverse the orientation of the remaining components $\{C_i\}_{i=1}^{p-w_C}$ to create a new oriented folded surface $X'$. Let $K$ be one of the singular arcs on the boundary of $C$ and let $N(K)$ be a regular neighbourhood of $K$ in $M$. The embedding $N(K)\cap X'\rightarrow N(K)$ is homeomorphic to the embedding of trivial sub-bundles $K_{2p-2w_C,1}\times S^1 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2\times S^1$ where the embedding restricts on sections to the embedding $K_{2p-2w_C,1}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2$ whose image in the unit disk is $2p-2w_C$ unit intervals $\{[0,x_j]\}_{j=1}^{2p-2w_C}$ where $x_j:= e^{\frac{2i\pi j}{2p-2w_C}}$ and $x_i \in C_i$ for all $1\leq i\leq p-w_C$ and $x_j \in (X\setminus C)^u$ for all $p-w_C< j\leq 2p-2w_C$. Fix an orientation of $\mathbb{D}^2$ in the splitting $\mathbb{D}^2\times S^1$. The orientations of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$ and $\mathbb{D}^2$ induce an orientation on the edges of the graph $X'\cap \mathbb{D}^2 \simeq K_{2p-2w_C,1}$ such that the intervals $[0,x_j]$ where $1\leq j \leq p-w_C$ induce the opposite orientation on the endpoint $0$ to the intervals where $p-w_C < j \leq 2p-2w_C$. Replace $X'\cap N(K)$ with the proper embedding of annuli given by the sub-bundle $\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{p-w_C} I_i \right)\times S^1 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2\times S^1$ which is described on sections as the proper embedding intervals $I_i := [x_i,x_{2p-2w_C-i+1}]$ in $\mathbb{D}^2$ where $1\leq i \leq p-w_C$. Orient $I_i$ such that it induces the same orientation on its endpoints $x_i,x_{2p-2w_C-i+1}$ as the sum of the edges $[0,x_i]$ and $[0,x_{2p-2w_C-i+1}]$ in the embedding $K_{2p-2w_C,1}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{D}^2$. This induces an orientation of the annuli $\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{p-w_C} I_i \right)\times S^1$ such that the orientation induced on their boundary is counter to the orientation induced by $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X')\cap {M\setminus N(K)}$ hence preserving orientability of the resulting folded surface. Perform these replacements to every singular arc on the boundary of $C$ and call the resulting folded surface $Y'$. Orient $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(Y')$ such that its orientation is consistent with $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X')$ wherever the two overlap.
    
    From the construction above we have that 
    \[|\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y'))| = |\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X^u))|- |\pi_0(\partial{C})|.\] 
    Additionally, $Y'$ differs from $X^u$ only in a regular neighbourhood of $C$ homeomorphic to a handlebody $H$ of genus $2g(C) + n(C) -1$ where $g(C)$ and $n(C)$ are the genus and number of boundary components of $\overline{C}$. A singular homology argument therefore implies that $[Y']- [X^u] \in \text{Im}(H_2(H;\mathbb{Z}_p)\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)) = \{0\}$ since $H_2(H;\mathbb{Z}_p) = 0$ and so $[Y'] = [X^u] = [X]$ as required. 

    By assumption there are no removable disks in $X$ and so Lemma~\ref{lem:removabledisksorclosed} implies that $\chi(C_{cut})\leq 0$. $X'_{cut}$ is obtained from $X^u_{cut}$ by deleting $2w_C - p$ components of Euler characteristic $\chi(C)$ and so $\chi_-(X') = \chi_-(X^u) - (2w_C -p)\chi_-(C)\leq \chi_-(X^u)$. $Y'_{cut}$ is obtained from $X'_{cut}$ by attaching $p-w_C$ annuli at each singular circle in $\partial C$ between pairs of boundary components $B_1,B_2$ belonging to components $S_j\in \pi_0(X'_{cut})$ for $j \in \{1,2\}$. The component of $X^u$ containing the $C_i$ has no removable disks and is not a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-crosscap and so Lemma~\ref{lem:removabledisksorclosed} implies that $\chi(S_j)\leq 0$. Let $S$ be the compact 2-manifold obtained by identifying the boundary of an annulus to $B_1$ and $B_2$ of disjoint $S_1$ and $S_2$. An elementary Euler characteristic computation shows that $\chi(S) = \chi(S_1)+\chi(S_2)\leq 0$. It follows that $\chi_-(S) = \chi_-(S_1)+\chi_-(S_2)$. If $S_1 = S_2$ then $\chi(S) = \chi(S_1)\leq 0$ which implies that $\chi_-(S) = \chi_-(S_1)$. Inductively applying these statements to every annulus in the construction this shows that $\chi_-(Y') = \chi_-(X')\leq \chi_-(X^u)$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} to $Y'$ now completes the proof.

If $p>2$ then there exists a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ with no removable disks such that $[Y] = [X]$ and $\chi(Y^u)\geq \chi(X^u)$ with strict inequality if $X$ has a removable disk. title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $X$ is a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface with a removable disk $D$. If $p>2$ since $p$ is an odd prime we have that $w_D<p/2$ so the removal of $D$ as per Lemma~\ref{lem:noremovabledisks} results in a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ such that $[Y] = [X]$, $\chi(Y^u) = \chi(X^u) + p-2w_D > \chi(X^u)$ and $Y$ has fewer singular arcs than $X$. The number of singular arcs in $X$ is finite so iterating we obtain a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ with no removable disks and such that $\chi(Y^u)>\chi(X^u)$.

    If $p=2$ then the removal of $D$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:noremovabledisks} strictly reduces the number of singular arcs and has no effect on the number of components of $M\setminus X$, the maximum weight of components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$, or the Euler characteristic. Repeatedly removing disks thus will terminate in a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-folded surface $Y$ with no removable disks such that $\chi(Y) = \chi(X)$.

label: lem:eulercharbounds
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:eulercharbounds}
    Let $M$ be a closed orientable 3-manifold. $\chi_p(x)\leq p\cdot \beta_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ for all $x\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X$ be a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface embedded in $M$ such that $[X] = x$. Lemma~\ref{lem:noremovablediskschi} implies that there exists another reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X_0$ realising the same homology class, with no removable disks and such that $\chi(X_0^u)\geq \chi(X^u)$. Let $Y$ be any connected component of $\underline{X_0}$ inheriting the weights of $X_0$. 
    
    Suppose $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y) = \emptyset$. Then $\underline{Y}$ is a closed connected oriented surface so $\chi(\underline{Y}) \leq 2$. $Y^u$ is constructed by pushing $\underline{Y}$ in a normal direction to generate $w_{\underline{Y}}\leq p/2$ parallel copies so $\chi(Y^u) = w_{\underline{Y}}\cdot \chi(\underline{Y}) \leq w_{\underline{Y}} \cdot 2 \leq p$.

    Suppose $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(Y) \neq \emptyset$. Since we assumed that there are no removable disks in $Y$, it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:removabledisksorclosed} that if any component of $Y_{cut}$ is homeomorphic to a disk then $Y^u$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-crosscap and $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(Y)$ consists of a single component of weight $1$ and $\chi(Y^u)=1$. Conversely if no component of $Y_{cut}$ is a disk then every component has non-positive Euler characteristic and so $\chi(Y^u)\leq 0$. 
    
    Hence in general for any $Y \in \pi_0(X_0)$ it follows that $\chi(Y^u)\leq p$. Lemma~\ref{lem:components} implies that the number of such connected components of $\underline{X_0}$ is bounded by the dimension of $H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$ as a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-vector space. Hence 
    \[\chi(X^u)\leq \chi(X_0^u) = \sum_{Y\in \pi_0(X)}\chi(Y^u) \leq p\cdot \beta_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p).\] 
    This completes the proof.

label: lem:equatingfunctions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:equatingfunctions}
    If $H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p) = \mathbb{Z}_p$, then $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p} = \max(-\chi_p(x),0)$ for all $x\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_p)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X$ be a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface in $M$ with no removable disks such that $[X] = x$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:reduced}). If $x=0$ then $\chi_p(0) = ||0||_{\mathbb{Z}_p}=0$ satisfies the equality trivially. 
    
    Now assume that $x\neq 0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:components} implies that $\underline{X}$ must be connected since it is non-separating and non-empty. The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:eulercharbounds} shows that $\chi(X^u)>0$ in precisely two cases \- when $X^u$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-crosscap and when $X^u$ is a disjoint union of $w_{\underline{X}} \leq p/2$ parallel $2$-spheres. In both cases $\chi_-(X^u) = 0 = \max(-\chi(X^u),0)$. 

    If $\chi(X^u)\leq 0$ then $\underline{X}$ cannot be a $2$-sphere and no component of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$ can be a disk due to Lemma~\ref{lem:removabledisksorclosed}. This implies that $\chi(C)\leq 0$ for all $C \in \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X^u_{cut}))$. By definition $\chi_-(X^u) = \chi_-(X^u_{cut}) = -\chi(X^u_{cut}) = -\chi(X^u) = \max(-\chi(X^u),0)$. 

    Now take the minimum of both sides of the equation 
    \[\chi_-(X^u) = \max(-\chi(X^u),0)\] 
    where $X$ runs over all reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surfaces realising $x$ with no removable disks. Lemma~\ref{lem:reduced} implies that the left hand side equates to $||x||_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:noremovablediskschi} implies that the right hand side equates to $\max(-\chi_p(x),0)$, completing the proof.

label: lem:normalpfoldsarereduced
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normalpfoldsarereduced}
    For each canonical $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $S_{\varphi}(\mathcal{T})$ there exists a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X$ such that $[X] = [S_{\varphi}(\mathcal{T})]$ and $\chi(X^u) = \chi(S_{\varphi}(\mathcal{T}))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\underline{X} = S_{\varphi}$ and $w_C = 1$ for every $C \in \pi_0(\text{Int}(\underline{X}))$. If $\underline{X}$ is non-separating in $M$ then we are done.

    Otherwise, there must exist a component $N$ of $M \setminus \underline{X}$ that does not contain the single vertex of $\mathcal{T}$. Let $\mathfrak{t}$ be the image of a tetrahedron of $\mathcal{T}$ and let $N'$ be a connected component of $N\cap\mathfrak{t}$. Recall that the intersection $X \cap \mathfrak{t}$ consists of normal $p$-folds or normal disks but not both (see Section~\ref{sec:normalpfoldedsurfacesconstruction}) and so up to isotopy and reversal of orientation of $\partial(N')\subset S_{\varphi} \cap \mathfrak{t}$ there are precisely $5$ possibilities for $N',\partial(N') \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{t}$ pictured in Figure~\ref{fig:N'intersectionwitht}.
    
    Let $N_+$ (resp. $N_-$) be the subsets of $\text{Int}(S_{\varphi}) \cap \partial N$ on the boundary of $N$ with consistent (resp. inconsistent) orientation with the orientation induced by $N\subset M$. Following the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} we can obtain a new weighted $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $Y$ by decreasing the weights of components of $N_+$ by one and increasing the weights of components of $N_-$ by one. The five cases in Figure~\ref{fig:N'intersectionwitht} clearly show that there is a cell decomposition of $\overline{N_+}$ and $\overline{N_-}$ with the same number of $2$-cells and $1$-cells. For each edge $e$ of $\mathcal{T}$ the degree of the vertices in $e\cap N_+$ and $e \cap N_-$ in the cell decompositions is equal to the degree of $e$ in $\mathcal{T}$ and so the number of $0$-cells is also the same. Hence $\chi(N_+) = \chi(N_-)$ and so $\chi(Y^u) = \chi(X^u) + \chi(N_-) - \chi(N_+) = \chi(X^u)$. Set $X=Y$. Repeat this process fixing $N$ until the number of components of $M \setminus \underline{X}$ decreases, then set $N$ to be another component of $M \setminus \underline{X}$ that does not contain the vertex of $\mathcal{T}$. Iterate until $M \setminus \underline{X}$ is connected. 
    
    Once this is complete $X$ is clearly a non-separating weighted surface with the property that $\chi(X^u) = \chi(S_{\varphi}(\mathcal{T}))$. Singular homology arguments from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} imply that $[X] = [S_{\varphi}(\mathcal{T})]$. For every edge $e$ of $\mathcal{T}$ oriented such that $\tilde{\varphi}(e)\geq 0$ it is also clear from the proof that the sum of the weights of the components of $\text{Int}(\underline{X})$ intersecting $e$ is $\tilde{\varphi}(e)$ at every step. In particular since $\tilde{\varphi}(e)<p/2$ this bounds every weight and shows that $X$ is also a reduced $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface as required.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I(x)\subset \pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X))$ be the set of components such that 
    \[H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H_2(X,\text{Sing}(X);\mathbb{Z}_2)=\mathbb{Z}_2[\pi_0(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X))]\] 
    maps $x \mapsto \sum_{C \in I(x)} C$. Let $S(x)$ be the sub-polyhedron given by $\overline{\bigcup I(x)}$. The number of sheets of $I(x)$ cobounding each arc of $S(x)\cap \text{Sing}(X)$ must be even since $\sum_{C \in I(x)} C$ is in the kernel of the connecting homomorphism $H_2(X,\text{Sing}(X);\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H_1(\text{Sing}(X);\mathbb{Z}_2)$. Since $X$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface this even number must be $0$ or $2$ and this is sufficient to show that $S(x)$ is a closed $2$-manifold. 

    Now let $f^{S(x)}:S(x)\rightarrow M$, $i^{S(x)}:S(x)\rightarrow X$ and $f^X:X\rightarrow M$ be the three embeddings such that $f^{S(x)} = f^X\circ i^{S(x)}$. Let $[S(x)]\in H_2(S(x);\mathbb{Z}_2)$ be the fundamental class of $S(x)$. The composition of maps $H_2(S(x);\mathbb{Z}_2)\xrightarrow{i^{S(x)}_*} H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_2) \hookrightarrow H_2(X,\text{Sing}(X);\mathbb{Z}_2)$ clearly sends $[S(x)]\mapsto \sum_{C \in I(x)} C$. The second map is an injection by a dimension argument and so we deduce that $x = i^{S(x)}_*([S])$. 
    
    Now if $x\in \ker(f^X_*:H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_2))$ then it follows that $f^{S(x)}_*([S]) = f^X_*\circ i^{S(x)}_*([S]) = f^X_*(x) = 0$. It is well known and easily verified that homologically trivial closed surfaces in $3$-manifolds are orientable. It follows immediately that any $C\in I(x)$ must be removable since if any two boundary arcs of $\partial C_{cut}$ are identified with the same singular arc $\alpha$ in $X$ then we can find a simple closed curve embedded in $\overline{C}$ intersecting $\alpha$ transversally once whose regular neighbourhood in $\overline{C}$ is a M\"obius band.

label: lem:surfaceelimination
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of this lemma uses the same tricks as Lemmas~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} and~\ref{lem:removenotdisks}. First view $X$ as a weighted $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface by assigning weights of $1$ to all components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$. Let $X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})$ be the result of deleting the components in $I(x,\mathfrak{o})$ and setting weights $w_D = 2$ for all $D\in I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ then the same reasoning in Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedpfoldedsurfaces} implies that $[X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})] = [X]$ since they differ by the trivial $H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_3)$ class represented by $S(x)$ with orientation $\mathfrak{o}$. Let $I_0(x)$ be the set of components in $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X)$ cobounding a singular arc in $S(x)$ that are not in $I(x)$. Clearly since $S(x)$ is a closed surface we can deduce that every component of $S(x)\cap \text{Sing}(X)$ is cobounded by precisely one component of $I_0(x)$, one component of $I(x,\mathfrak{o})$ and one component of $I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$, all inducing a consistent orientation on their shared boundary.
    
    This means that if we take $X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})$, reverse the orientation of the components of $I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ and set their weights equal to $1$ then the two components cobounding each arc of $S(x)\cap \text{Sing}(X)$ now induce opposite orientations along their shared boundary and have the same weight. We can therefore extend the inverted orientation of $\bigsqcup I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ and the original orientation of $\bigsqcup I^0(x)$ to an orientation of $2$-manifold obtained by gluing them along $S(x)\cap\text{Sing}(X)$. We remove $S(x)\cap\text{Sing}(X)$ from the singular locus and call the resulting oriented folded surface $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$. To see that $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface simply note that the neighbourhoods and orientations of points outside of a regular neighbourhood of $\bigsqcup I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ are identical to in $X$ and inside this regular neighbourhood $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$ is an oriented $2$-manifold. 
    
    The image of $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$ and its orientation data in $M$ is identical to $(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o}))^u$ outside a regular neighbourhood of each component in $I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$. 
    
    Let $\Sigma$ be a closed $2$-manifold component of $I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ with the orientation inherited from $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$ and let $[Sigma]\in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_3)$ be the class represented by $\Sigma$. The component of the weighted $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface $X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})$ with underlying set $\Sigma$ has the opposite orientation and weight $2$ so it represents the class $-2[\Sigma] \in H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_3)$. These two classes are equivalent because $1\equiv -2 \mod 3$. It follows that the change made to closed $2$-manifold components does not affect the class represented.
    
    Let $H$ be a regular neighbourhood of $\bigsqcup_{D\in I(x,-\mathfrak{o}), \partial D \neq \emptyset} \overline{D}$. Since each $\overline{D}$ is a compact $2$-manifold with non-empty boundary it has a regular neighbourhood homeomorphic to a handlebody. $H$ is a disjoint union of handlebodies and so $H_2(H;\mathbb{Z}_3) = 0$. It follows from this that the change made to the components of $X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})$ with non-empty boundary also does not affect the class represented.
    
    It follows from these observations that $[X(x,\mathfrak{o})] = [X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})] = [X]$.

    A dimension argument can be used to show that the inclusion $X(x,\mathfrak{o})\subset X$ induces an injection 
    \[H_2(X(x,\mathfrak{o});\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_2).\] 
    Moreover it is clear that $x$ is not in the image of this homomorphism since $S(x)\not \subset X(x,\mathfrak{o})$. Finally, $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$ has the same image set as $\underline{X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})}$ and so
    \[\chi(X(x,\mathfrak{o})) = \chi(\underline{X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})}) = \chi(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o}))).\] 
    Recall that the only components of $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o}))$ with weight not equal to $1$ are those in $I(x,-\mathfrak{o})$ which have weight $2$ and so 
    \[\chi(\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o}))) = \chi(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})^u) - \sum_{D \in I(x,-\mathfrak{o})}\chi(D).\] 
    Counting the multiplicities of interior components we can obtain 
    \[\chi(X_0(x,\mathfrak{o})^u) = \chi(X)- \sum_{C\in I(x,\mathfrak{o})}\chi(C) + \sum_{D\in I(x,-\mathfrak{o})}\chi(D).\] 
    Combining these statements yields the desired Euler characteristic 
    \[\chi(X(x,\mathfrak{o})) = \chi(X) - \sum_{C\in I(x,\mathfrak{o})}\chi(C).\] 

    The fact that the inclusion 
    \[i_{(X,X(x,\mathfrak{o}))}:H_2(X(x,\mathfrak{o});\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}_2)\] 
    identifies $\ker i_{(M,X(x,\mathfrak{o}))}$ with a proper subgroup of $\ker i_{(M,X)}$ follows from noting the fact that $x$ cannot be in the image of $i_{(X,X(x,\mathfrak{o}))}$ since the class
    \[j_{(X,\operatorname{\text{Sing}} X)}(x) \in H_2(X,\operatorname{\text{Sing}} X;\mathbb{Z}_2)\] 
    is supported by the classes of components of $I(x,\mathfrak{o})$ that are not in $X(x,\mathfrak{o})$.

title: Proof

label: lem:changingcorecircle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:changingcorecircle}

    Let $L$ be a lens space with a splitting torus $T$ and let $C$ be a core circle of one of the solid tori of $L\setminus T$. Let $h_t:L\rightarrow L$ be an ambient isotopy of $L$. Let $T_1$ be the torus given by the boundary of a regular neighbourhood (the star) of the circle $h_1(C)$. Then there exists a homeomorphism $g:L\rightarrow L$ such that $g(T) = T_1$. title: Proof
body_md: Let $T_0$ be the torus boundary of a regular neighbourhood of $C$. $T_0$ and $T$ cobound a thickened torus and this can be used to construct an isotopy carrying $T$ to $T_0$. This can be extended to an ambient isotopy $\psi_t: L\rightarrow L$ by the PL isotopy extension theorem (see~\cite{hudson1966}) such that $\psi_1(T) = T_0$. The tori $h_1(T_0)$ and $T_1$ are the boundaries of two regular neighbourhoods of the same circle $h_1(C)$ given by different simplicial structures of $L$. The uniqueness of regular neighbourhoods implies that there exists a homeomorphism $f:L\rightarrow L$ such that $f|_{h_1(C)} = id$ and $f(h_1(T_0)) = T_1$. In particular if we set $g = f\circ h_1 \circ \psi_1$ we have a homeomorphism of $L$ such that $g(T) = T_1$ as required.

\label{thm:relmocktransversality}
    Let $P$ and $Q$ be proper subpolyhedra of a compact $n$-manifold $M$, with $P\cap \partial M$ mocktransverse to $Q\cap \partial M$ in the $n-1$-manifold $\partial M$. There exists an arbitrarily small ambient isotopy $h_t$ of $M$ such that $h_t|_{\partial M} = id$ for all $t$ and $h_1(P)$ is mocktransverse to $Q$.

label: lem:meridionaldiskintersection
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C_1$ be a core circle of the solid torus $S_1$ in the genus $1$ Heegaard splitting $L(k,q)=S_1\cup S_2$. Theorem~\ref{thm:relmocktransversality} implies that there exists an ambient isotopy $h_t$ of $L(k,q)$ such that $h_1(C_1)$ is mocktransverse to $X$. Use Lemma~\ref{lem:changingcorecircle} to replace $S_1$ with a closed regular neighbourhood of $h_1(C_1)$ and $S_2$ with the closure of its complement. It follows from a dimension argument that $h_1(C_1)$ intersects $X$ only at points in $\text{Int}(X)$ and that these intersections are locally transverse (i.e. locally modelled by $\mathbb{R}\times \{0\}\times \{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}$). It follows from considering the intersection of $S_1$ with these local neighbourhoods of intersection points that $X$ intersects the new $S_1$ in a disjoint union of meridional disks and that there is at least a local bicollaring of $(\partial S_1,X\cap \partial S_1)$ in $L(k,q)$. This local bicollaring extends to a global bicollaring since in particular $\partial S_1$ is the boundary of a regular neighbourhood and so must have a trivial normal bundle in $L(k,q)$.
    
    Now orient these disks with the orientation inherited from $\text{Int}(X)$ and fix a meridional homology class $\mu_1 \in H_1(\partial(S_1);\mathbb{Z})$. Let $[\mu_1]$ be the image of $\mu_1$ under the change of coefficients $H_1(\partial S_1;\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_1(\partial S_1;\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$. The Mayer-Vietoris sequence on the homology of $L(k,q),S_1,S_2$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ yields a well defined map $\partial_*:H_2(L(k,q);\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H_1(\partial S_1;\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ which sends $[X]\mapsto (d_+-d_-)[\mu_1]$. The subgroup generated by $[\mu_1]$ is $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ so this determines the $\mod p$ equivalence class of $d_+-d_-$. Moreover since $H_2(S_1;\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})\oplus H_2(S_2;\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})\cong 0$ the exactness of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence yields that $\ker \partial_*=0$ and so this class is unique.

\label{dfn:pfoldedwbdry}
    $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded $1$-manifolds are the boundaries of \textit{$\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surfaces with boundary} which can be defined by broadening the definition of a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface $X$ to include two new neighbourhood types: $[0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ and $[0,\infty) \times K_{p,1}$. The boundary $\partial X$ is the complement of the points of $X$ that have local neighbourhoods given in the original Definition~\ref{dfn:pfoldedsurface}. If we let $v$ be the $p$-valent vertex of $K_{p,1}$ then we define $\operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ as the set of points locally modelled by $(0,v)$ in either $[0,\infty) \times K_{p,1}$ or $\mathbb{R} \times K_{p,1}$ such that $\partial \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X) = Sing(X) \cap \partial X$. We define $\operatorname{\text{Int}}(X):= X\setminus \operatorname{\text{Sing}}(X)$ as before. A $\mathbb{Z}_p$-folded surface with boundary $X$ is \textit{properly embedded} in a $3$-manifold with boundary $M,\partial M$ when $X\cap \partial M = \partial X$.

\label{lem:boundaryvertexpattern}
    Suppose $(D,\Gamma_X)$ is a meridional intersection pattern of $X\hookrightarrow L(k,q) = S_1\cup S_2$ and that $X\cap S_1$ consists of $d$ meridional disks. Let $\sigma$ be the permutation of $X\cap \partial D = \partial(\Gamma_X)$ described in Lemma~\ref{lem:transversemeridionaldisk}. The orientation of $b\in \partial(\Gamma_X)$ induced by the orientation of $\text{Int}(\Gamma_X)$ is the same as the orientation of $\sigma^d(b)$.

title: Proof
body_md: Let $B_2$ be the $3$-ball described in Definition~\ref{dfn:meridionalintersectionpattern} and let $A$ be the annular preimage of $T = S_1\cap S_2$ under the quotient map $B_2\xrightarrow{f} S_2$. The orientation of $\text{Int}(X)\cap S_2$ induces an orientation on the union of curves $X\cap \partial S_2$ that intersect $\partial D$ mocktransversally as per Lemma~\ref{lem:transversemeridionaldisk}. With this orientation, $f^{-1}(X\cap T)$ is a disjoint union of oriented intervals, each of which has one endpoint in $\partial(\tilde{\Gamma}_X)$. For each $b \in \partial(\Gamma_X)$ let $\tilde{b}\in \partial(\tilde{\Gamma}_X)$ be the point identified to it by $f$. Let $I$ be the interval in $f^{-1}(X\cap T)$ that cobounds $\tilde{b}$ and $J$ be the interval in $\text{Int}(\tilde{\Gamma}_X)$. Since $(T,X\cap T)$ collars in $(S_2,X\cap S_2)$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:meridionaldiskintersection}) we can deduce that $I$ and $J$ are both intervals of the boundary of the same oriented component of $f^{-1}(\text{Int}(X)\cap S_2)$ and so must induce opposite orientations on the vertex $\tilde{b}$ they both cobound. The orientation that $I$ induces on $\tilde{b} = I\cap \partial \tilde{D}$ determines the sign of the intersection of $X\cap T$ with $\partial D$. The orientation induced on $X\cap T$ by the orientation of $\text{Int}(X)\cap S_2$ is the opposite of the orientation induced by $X\cap S_1$ and it remains true with either choice that the sign of the intersection of $X\cap T$ with $\partial D$ at any point $b\in \partial(\Gamma_X)$ determines the orientation of $b$ induced by the orientation of $\text{Int}(X)$. The proof is completed by applying Lemma~\ref{lem:transversemeridionaldisk}.

title: Proof
body_md: Let $E$ be a component of $D\setminus \Gamma_X$ as described. If $E$ cobounds a simple closed curve in $\Gamma_X$ then $E$ is a $0$-compression disk. Similarly if $E$ cobounds a cycle of length $2$ or $4$ in $\Gamma_X$ then $E$ is a $2$ or $4$-compression disk respectively. Accordingly let $X'$ be the result of performing a reduced $2k$-compression of $X$ about $E$ where $k\in \{0,1,2\}$ as necessary (see Section~\ref{sec:reducedsurgeries} for details). The regular neighbourhood of $E$ used in the surgery can be taken to be a subcomplex of the bicollar $[-1,1]\times D$ such that the two parallel disks are $\{1\}\times E$ and $\{-1\}\times E$. The fact that $(D,D \cap X')$ still bicollars in $(S_2,X'\cap S_2)$ follows from taking a slightly smaller collar $[-1+\varepsilon,1 - \varepsilon]\times D$ and noting that in this collar $\text{Int}(X')$ is a subset of the components of $\text{Int}(X)$. The effect of $2k$-compressions on the meridional intersection pattern is summarised in Figure~\ref{fig:meridionalsurgeries}. When embedded orientable surfaces are removed as part of the reduction of these surgeries to recover a non-separating $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface it is possible that the result will be an even simpler meridional intersection pattern with fewer interior components and singular vertices and some of the meridional disks in the intersection with $S_1$ may also be eliminated.

label: lem:floatingcomponents
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:floatingcomponents}
    Let $\Gamma$ be a connected finite trivalent bipartite multigraph embedded in the plane. There exists an open disk component of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus \Gamma$ that is bounded by a cycle of two or four edges in $\Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider the embedding $\Gamma \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2\hookrightarrow S^2$ via the one point compactification and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the cell decomposition of $S^2$ induced by $\Gamma$ such that $\mathcal{C}^{(1)}=\Gamma$. All but one of the $2$-cells in $\mathcal{C}^{(2)}$ lift to a disk in $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus \Gamma$. Let $c_{2k}$ be the number of $2$-cells of $\mathcal{C}^{(2)}$ cobounding a $2k$-cycle in $\Gamma$. Each edge in $\Gamma$ occurs exactly twice in the boundaries of these $2$-cells and each vertex occurs exactly three times. From this observation it follows from computing the Euler characteristic by counting cells that:
    
    \begin{align*}
        2  &= \chi(S^2)\\
        &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} c_{2k} - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2k c_{2k} + \frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2k c_{2k} \\
        &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1-\frac{k}{3})c_{2k}\\
    \end{align*}
    
    This implies that $2c_2 + c_4 \geq 6$ and so $c_2+c_4 \geq 3$. Since there are at least three $2$-cells that are bounded by cycles of length $2$ or $4$ it follows that at least two of these do not contain the point at $\infty$ and therefore lift to open disks in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Gamma$ that bound cycles of length $2$ or $4$ as required.

title: Proof
body_md: This follows from a standard inner-most disk style argument to find a component $G$ of $\Gamma_X$ contained in the interior of $D$ such that every other component of $\Gamma_X$ is contained in a single open annulus component of $D\setminus G$. label: lem:intervalbetterintersection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:intervalbetterintersection}
    Let $X$ be a $\chi$-optimal $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface embedded in $L(3n,q)$ with $S_1\cup S_2$ adapted to $X$ such that $X\cap S_1$ consists of $d>1$ meridional disks and $(D,\Gamma_X)$ is an intersection pattern of $X$ of the kind described in Lemma~\ref{lem:simplifiedwithsurgieries}. There exists an interval $I$ properly embedded in $D$ such that $I$ intersects $\Gamma_X$ locally transversally at points in $\text{Int}(\Gamma_X)$ and such that there is an arc $I'$ in $\partial D$ such that $\partial I' = \partial I$ and $|I\cap \Gamma_X| < |I'\cap \Gamma_X| \leq d$. Moreover there exists an equivalent genus $1$ Heegaard decomposition $S_1'\cup S_2'$ of $L(3n,q)$ adapted to $X$ such that $X\cap S_1'$ consists of fewer than $d$ meridional disks.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:simplifiedl3nqintersectionpattern} is a straightforward induction on the number of meridional disks. The general structure of the argument is as follows:
    
    We start with any $\chi$-optimal $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface $X$ embedded in a lens space with a genus $1$ Heegaard decomposition $S_1\cup S_2$ and a meridional intersection pattern $(D,\Gamma_X)$. Fixing $S_1,S_2,D$ we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:simplifiedwithsurgieries} to replace $X$ with another $\chi$-optimal $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface whose corresponding meridional intersection pattern has been maximally simplified with the reduced compression surgeries described in Section~\ref{sec:reducedsurgeries}. If $X\cap S_1$ consists of more than one meridional disk then we fix $X$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:intervalbetterintersection} to replace $S_1,S_2$ with an equivalent genus $1$ Heegaard decomposition adapted to $X$ such that now $S_1\cap X$ consists of strictly fewer meridional disks. We then use Lemma~\ref{lem:transversemeridionaldisk} to obtain a new mock-transverse meridional disk $D$ that determines a new meridional intersection pattern as per Definition~\ref{dfn:meridionalintersectionpattern}. 

    Repeatedly applying Lemmas~\ref{lem:simplifiedwithsurgieries}, ~\ref{lem:intervalbetterintersection} and ~\ref{lem:transversemeridionaldisk} results in a $\chi$-optimal $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surface, adapted genus $1$ Heegaard splitting and meridional intersection pattern $(D,\Gamma_X)$ with the required properties.
